newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's King Simeon urges early elections.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's King Simeon urges early elections.

text.p: Bulgaria's exiled King Simeon II said on Friday he supported opposition demands for early general elections as the only democratic way out of the grave political and economic crisis battering the country.
In a statement released by his press office in Sofia he urged Bulgarian politicians to set a date for early elections as soon as possible to avoid further devastation.

"The more time you waste on unworthy deals and postpone the date for early elections under the pretext of making politics, the greater the danger of unpredictable consequences," said Simeon, now a Madrid-based business consultant.

After 12 days of massive protests, the Socialist government, composed largely of ex-communists, and the opposition are calling for talks to break a political and economic impasse but are still far apart on details.
The Socialists, blamed for mishandling the economy, say they want negotiations with the opposition but hope to delay until the end of this year polls likely to sweep them from power if held sooner.
The opposition, led by deputies of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), are boycotting parliament until their demands to hold general elections soon are met.
Vital talks with the International Monetary Fund on implementation of a strict monetary regime aimed to help the crumbling economy recover have been postponed until Sofia appoints a new government.

"The lack of political sense...the lack of will on behalf of the ruling party to observe the rules of the democratic political game...the disregard for the suffering of the people, make it responsible for the current tension," said Simeon's statement.
"In every democratic country early elections function as a vent and are accepted practice when the ruling party has disappointed the people," he added.
Now 59, Simeon fled Bulgaria as a child in 1946 after the Soviet Red Army installed a puppet communist regime.
He returned to Bulgaria for the first time in 50 years for a three-week visit in May last year and was mobbed by an ecstatic flag-waving public.
"The patience shown by Bulgarians in the past year was surprising given the serious reasons for discontent among the mistreated population," said Simeon.
Millions have been plunged into poverty by inflation of over 300 percent and a currency collapse blamed on the government's failure to implement reforms.
An opinion poll on Thursday gave the Socialists just eight percent support.

"We are all witness to what Bulgaria was turned into by mediocrity, egoism, greed and power hunger," said Simeon, who as a Saxe-Coburg is related to other European royal families, including Britain's House of Windsor.

Simeon never renounced his claim to the throne. The balding, bearded monarch is respected even by republicans as a serious, hard-working businessman who eschews the playboy lifestyle of some exiled royals.
